plain_english: Whatever you put serious effort into, you naturally love. Do people put serious effort into bad things? No way. Do they put effort into things that don't matter to them at all? No, not those either. So people only put real effort into good things. And if they're putting effort into something, they love it too. Anyone who truly understands what's good can also know how to love. But someone who can't tell good from bad, or figure out what's neither good nor bad — how could they know how to love? Only wise people can truly love.
original_excerpt: What a man applies himself to earnestly, that he naturally loves. Do men then apply themselves earnestly to the things which are bad? By no means. Well, do they apply themselves to things which in no way concern themselves? Not to these either. It remains then that they employ themselves earnestly only about things which are good; and if they are earnestly employed about things, they love such things also. Whoever then understands what is good can also know how to love; but he who cannot distinguish good from bad, and things which are neither good nor bad from both, how can he possess the power of loving? To love, then, is only in the power of the wise.

plain_english: Don't fool yourself — every creature cares about nothing more than its own interests. Whatever seems to block those interests, it will hate. Doesn't matter if it's a brother, father, child, beloved, or lover. The creature will reject them, push them away, curse them. This is just nature — nothing matters more than self-interest. Self-interest is father, brother, family, country, and God all rolled into one. So when the gods seem to block what we want, we curse them. We tear down their statues. We burn their temples. Just like Alexander ordered the temples of Aesculapius burned when his dear friend died.
original_excerpt: For universally, be not deceived, every animal is attached to nothing so much as to its own interests. Whatever then appears to it an impediment to this interest, whether this be a brother, or a father, or a child, or beloved, or lover, it hates, spurns, curses; for its nature is to love nothing so much as its own interests: this is father, and brother, and kinsman, and country, and God. When then the gods appear to us to be an impediment to this, we abuse them and throw down their statues and burn their temples, as Alexander ordered the temples of Aesculapius to be burned when his dear friend died.

plain_english: Here's the key: if you put your true interest in the same place as your integrity, goodness, country, parents, and friends, then all of these are safe. But if you put your interest in one place and your friends, country, family, and justice in another place, then all of these will be trampled. They get crushed under the weight of your selfish interest. Whatever you care about most — that's where you'll naturally go. If you care most about physical pleasure, that rules you. If you care most about your choices and character, that rules you. If you care most about external things, that rules you. Only when I am where my will is — only then will I be the kind of friend I should be, and son, and father. Because then it will be in my interest to stay faithful, modest, patient, self-controlled, and helpful. It will be in my interest to honor my relationships. But if I put myself in one place and honesty in another, then Epicurus wins. His teaching says that either virtue doesn't exist, or virtue is just whatever people think is virtuous.
original_excerpt: For this reason, if a man put in the same place his interest, sanctity, goodness, and country, and parents, and friends, all these are secured: but if he puts in one place his interest, in another his friends, and his country and his kinsmen and justice itself, all these give way, being borne down by the weight of interest. For where the I and the Mine are placed, to that place of necessity the animal inclines; if in the flesh, there is the ruling power; if in the will, it is there; and if it is in externals, it is there. If then I am there where my will is, then only shall I be a friend such as I ought to be, and son, and father; for this will be my interest, to maintain the character of fidelity, of modesty, of patience, of abstinence, of active co-operation, of observing my relations (towards all). But if I put myself in one place, and honesty in another, then the doctrine of Epicurus becomes strong, which asserts either that there is no honesty or it is that which opinion holds to be honest (virtuous).

plain_english: This ignorance is what caused the Athenians and Spartans to fight each other. The Thebans fought both of them. The Persian king fought the Greeks, and the Macedonians fought both sides. The Romans fought the Getae. Even earlier, the Trojan War happened for the same reasons. Alexander was Menelaus's guest. If you had seen how friendly they were, you wouldn't have believed anyone who said they weren't friends. But something was thrown between them — like a piece of meat thrown between dogs. In this case, it was a beautiful woman. And that's what started the war.
original_excerpt: It was through this ignorance that the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians quarrelled, and the Thebans with both; and the great king quarrelled with Hellas, and the Macedonians with both: and the Romans with the Getae. And still earlier the Trojan war happened for these reasons. Alexander was the guest of Menelaus, and if any man had seen their friendly disposition, he would not have believed any one who said that they were not friends. But there was cast between them (as between dogs) a bit of meat, a handsome woman, and about her war arose.

plain_english: When you see brothers who seem friendly and claim they think alike, don't assume anything about their friendship. Don't believe them even if they swear they could never be separated. You can't trust the mind of a bad person. It's unstable. It has no solid principles to guide it. Different situations will push it in different directions. Don't look at what most people look at — whether they have the same parents, grew up together, or had the same teacher. Look at this instead: what do they really care about? Do they care about external things or about their own choices? If they care about externals, don't call them friends. Don't call them trustworthy, steady, brave, or free either. If you have any sense, don't even call them real human beings.
original_excerpt: And now when you see brothers to be friends appearing to have one mind, do not conclude from this anything about their friendship, not even if they swear it and say that it is impossible for them to be separated from one another. For the ruling principle of a bad man cannot be trusted; it is insecure, has no certain rule by which it is directed, and is overpowered at different times by different appearances. But examine, not what other men examine, if they are born of the same parents and brought up together, and under the same pedagogue; but examine this only, wherein they place their interest, whether in externals or in the will. If in externals, do not name them friends, no more than name them trustworthy or constant, or brave or free; do not name them even men, if you have any judgment.

plain_english:
What makes people bite each other, abuse each other, and fight over empty places or public spaces like wild animals? What makes them act like robbers in courtrooms? What makes them lustful, unfaithful, and corrupt? What makes them do all the terrible things they do to each other? It's one simple mistake: they put themselves and their interests in things they can't actually control.

But when you hear that people truly believe good things only exist where their will is — where they use their judgments correctly — then don't worry about whether they're your father, son, brothers, or old friends. Once you know this about them, you can confidently call them friends. You can say they're trustworthy and just. Where else can friendship exist except where there's loyalty, decency, and a shared commitment to honest things — and nothing else?
original_excerpt: For that is not a principle of human nature which makes them bite one another, and abuse one another, and occupy deserted places or public places, as if they were mountains, and in the courts of justice display the acts of robbers; nor yet that which makes them intemperate and adulterers and corrupters, nor that which makes them do whatever else men do against one another through this one opinion only, that of placing themselves and their interests in the things which are not within the power of their will. But if you hear that in truth these men think the good to be only there, where will is, and where there is a right use of appearances, no longer trouble yourself whether they are father or son, or brothers, or have associated a long time and are companions, but when you have ascertained this only, confidently declare that they are friends, as you declare that they are faithful, that they are just. For where else is friendship than where there is fidelity, and modesty, where there is a communion of honest things and of nothing else.

plain_english: But you might say, "This person treated me well for so long. Didn't he love me?" How do you know, fool, that he didn't regard you the same way he uses a sponge to wipe his shoes? Or the way he takes care of his livestock? How do you know that once you're no longer useful to him, he won't throw you away like a broken dish? "But this woman is my wife. We've lived together for years." So what? How long did Eriphyle live with Amphiaraus? She was the mother of his children — many of them. But a necklace came between them. And what is a necklace? It's just your opinion about such things. That was the animal instinct in her. That's what destroyed the friendship between husband and wife. That's what stopped the woman from being a wife and the mother from being a mother.
original_excerpt: But you may say, Such a one treated me with regard so long; and did he not love me? How do you know, slave, if he did not regard you in the same way as he wipes his shoes with a sponge, or as he takes care of his beast? How do you know, when you have ceased to be useful as a vessel, he will not throw you away like a broken platter? But this woman is my wife, and we have lived together so long. And how long did Eriphyle live with Amphiaraus, and was the mother of children and of many? But a necklace came between them: and what is a necklace? It is the opinion about such things. That was the bestial principle, that was the thing which broke asunder the friendship between husband and wife, that which did not allow the woman to be a wife nor the mother to be a mother.

plain_english: If you want to be a true friend or have true friends, you need to cut out certain toxic opinions. Hate them. Drive them from your soul. When you do this, you'll stop beating yourself up. You won't fight with yourself or keep changing your mind. You won't torture yourself. And with other people who think like you, you'll be a complete friend. With people who don't think like you, you'll still be patient. You'll be kind and gentle. You'll forgive them because they don't know better — they're just wrong about important things. But you won't be harsh with anyone. Remember what Plato taught: every mind loses truth against its will. If you can't manage this, you can still do what friends normally do. You can drink together, live together, travel together. You might even be born from the same parents. Snakes are born from the same parents too. But neither snakes nor you will be real friends as long as you hold onto these brutal, poisonous opinions.
original_excerpt: And let every man among you who has seriously resolved either to be a friend himself or to have another for his friend, cut out these opinions, hate them, drive them from his soul. And thus first of all he will not reproach himself, he will not be at variance with himself, he will not change his mind, he will not torture himself. In the next place, to another also, who is like himself, he will be altogether and completely a friend. But he will bear with the man who is unlike himself, he will be kind to him, gentle, ready to pardon on account of his ignorance, on account of his being mistaken in things of the greatest importance; but he will be harsh to no man, being well convinced of Plato's doctrine that every mind is deprived of truth unwillingly. If you cannot do this, yet you can do in all other respects as friends do, drink together, and lodge together, and sail together, and you may be born of the same parents, for snakes also are: but neither will they be friends, nor you, so long as you retain these bestial and cursed opinions.
